html:
Life size heads of copper alloy and terracotta made at Ile-Ife, in southwest Nigeria, mostly between the 12th and 15th centuries. Their calm, natural faces are among the masterpieces of world art.

Ife is the sacred city of the Yoruba, who say the world was created there and that their first king, Oduduwa, ruled from it. The heads probably show its kings, the Ooni, or people of the court. Many have fine parallel lines on the face, and small holes along the hairline and lips, perhaps for attaching beads or hair.

In 1910 the German explorer Leo Frobenius found a bronze head and claimed it must be Greek, the work of the lost Atlantis, because he could not believe Africans had made it. In 1938 workers digging a house foundation in Ife found eighteen more copper alloy heads. Their quality and realism forced Europeans to rethink their low view of African art.

The heads were cast by the lost wax method. They come between the earlier Igbo-Ukwu bronzes and the later Benin Bronzes, whose makers may have learned from Ife.
